clinicalPearls: Benign exophytic squamous papillomas of the larynx that are the laryngeal manifestation of recurrent respiratory papillomatosis, driven by human papillomavirus, chiefly types 6 and 11
Juvenile-onset disease presents in childhood with progressive hoarseness, an abnormal cry, and sometimes stridor, and tends to be more aggressive and multifocal
Adult-onset disease more often causes persistent dysphonia and follows a comparatively less florid course
Lesions favour anatomical transition zones, especially the true vocal folds and the limen vestibuli
Progressive stridor and airway obstruction from bulky disease can be life-threatening, particularly in young children
Treatment is repeated surgical debulking to preserve airway and voice while sparing normal mucosa, as recurrence is expected and cure elusive
Distal spread to the trachea and lungs and malignant transformation, more likely with type 11 or after prior irradiation, are recognised complications
reference.pathophysiology: Laryngeal papillomas are the airway expression of recurrent respiratory papillomatosis, in which human papillomavirus, predominantly the low-risk genotypes 6 and 11, infects the respiratory epithelium and drives proliferation of the basal squamous cells. Juvenile-onset disease is thought to result from vertical transmission during passage through an infected birth canal, whereas adult acquisition is less clearly defined. The virus persists within apparently normal-looking mucosa, which explains the characteristic tendency to recur after removal. Lesions cluster at squamociliary junctions and produce friable, frond-like growths that add mass to the vocal folds and, when bulky, obstruct the airway; rarely the process spreads distally or undergoes malignant change.
additionalDifferentials: Verrucous or invasive squamous cell carcinoma
Congenital laryngeal cyst (in the child with stridor)
additionalInvestigations: Flexible fibreoptic laryngoscopy to identify and map the papillomatous lesions
Rigid endoscopy under anaesthesia for assessment, mapping, and biopsy
Histopathology to confirm papilloma and exclude dysplasia or malignancy
Human papillomavirus typing of tissue, given prognostic relevance of type 11
Tracheobronchoscopy or imaging where distal airway or pulmonary spread is suspected
redFlags: Progressive stridor or airway obstruction, especially in a young child, which is potentially life-threatening
Rapid growth, keratinisation, or an ulcerated mass suggesting malignant transformation
Frequent recurrences requiring escalating numbers of procedures
reference.prognosis: The course is unpredictable and often chronic with repeated recurrences, and some childhood cases eventually remit spontaneously, but aggressive multifocal or distally spreading disease carries significant morbidity and a small but important risk of malignant transformation.
pitfalls: Aggressive deep resection that damages the vocal ligament and anterior commissure, risking scarring and web formation
Assuming complete surgical clearance eradicates the virus, when latent virus in normal mucosa drives recurrence
Overlooking malignant transformation in longstanding or type 11 disease
Neglecting airway planning in a child with bulky papillomas before anaesthesia
references: Cummings Otolaryngology: Head and Neck Surgery
Scott-Brown's Otorhinolaryngology, Head and Neck Surgery
management: The mainstay is repeated conservative surgical debulking with microdebrider or CO2 laser to maintain airway and voice while sparing normal mucosa, as recurrence is expected
Add adjuvant therapy in aggressive or frequently recurring disease, such as intralesional cidofovir or systemic bevacizumab, with HPV vaccination as an adjunct
Manage acute airway obstruction promptly, avoiding tracheostomy where possible because it risks distal seeding of papillomas
Provide voice therapy and support voice outcomes given the cumulative scarring from repeated procedures
Undertake surveillance endoscopy for recurrence, distal tracheobronchial or pulmonary spread, and malignant transformation, particularly with HPV type 11
Type HPV on excised tissue for prognostic stratification and confirm histology to exclude dysplasia
Coordinate ENT and respiratory specialist care with regular structured review
